t: OpenQuantumSafe: What OpenQuantumSafe Is: Crypto for the Quantum Age
title: OpenQuantumSafe: What OpenQuantumSafe Is: Crypto for the Quantum Age
description: liboqs implements the post-quantum algorithms NIST selected: ML-KEM (Kyber) for key establishment, ML-DSA (Dilithium) for signatures, plus SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) and FN-DSA (Falcon). It is the reference implementation teams integrate first — the C library, the OpenSSL provider (oqs-provider), and the OpenSSH fork that let you handshake with quantum-resistant crypto today. When Shor's algorithm eventually breaks RSA and ECC, these lattice- and hash-based schemes are the replacement.

title: OpenQuantumSafe: ML-KEM (Kyber): Key Encapsulation
description: ML-KEM (FIPS 203, ex-Kyber) is the key-establishment workhorse: the server publishes a public key, the client encapsulates a random secret to it, both derive the shared secret. Parameter sets 512/768/1024 trade security for size (public keys 800/1184/1568 bytes — bigger than ECC's 32, the price of quantum resistance). liboqs implements all three with constant-time code. The migration pattern is hybrid key exchange: X25519 plus ML-KEM-768, secure if either holds.

title: OpenQuantumSafe: ML-DSA (Dilithium): Signatures
description: ML-DSA (FIPS 204, ex-Dilithium) signs: parameter sets 44/65/87 with signatures around 2.4-4.6 KB — large next to ECDSA's 64 bytes, the cost of lattice security. liboqs implements all sets plus the stateless hash-based SLH-DSA for the paranoid (bigger, slower, minimal assumptions). Choosing is engineering: Dilithium for general use, SLH-DSA where the threat model justifies the cost. Signature sizes ripple through protocols — certificates, handshakes, and embedded budgets all feel it.

t: OpenQuantumSafe: The Threat: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later
title: OpenQuantumSafe: The Threat: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later
description: The urgency has a name: adversaries record encrypted traffic today to decrypt when cryptographically-relevant quantum computers arrive. Data with a long secrecy lifetime — state secrets, health records, infrastructure designs — is already exposed if it was encrypted with RSA/ECC and recorded. This is why migration cannot wait for the quantum computer: the attack is happening now, against the future. PQC migration is defense against a clock that is already running.

title: OpenQuantumSafe: Your First Handshake: oqs-provider
description: The hello-world: build oqs-provider, configure OpenSSL to load it, and negotiate a TLS handshake with ML-KEM-768 key exchange — s_client/s_server showing the PQC group in the cipher description. It works today, interoperably, with the hybrid groups. From there: the OpenSSH fork for PQC host keys, then liboqs in your own application. The handshake you can run this afternoon is the migration's proof of concept.

t: OpenQuantumSafe: liboqs API: Integrating PQC into Applications
title: OpenQuantumSafe: liboqs API: Integrating PQC into Applications
description: Beyond OpenSSL, liboqs integrates directly: the C API (OQS_KEM_keypair/encaps/decaps) drops PQC into custom protocols, VPNs, and embedded systems. The integration points are key generation (slow — do it rarely), encapsulation (fast), and the size budgets (keys and ciphertexts in your packet formats). The pattern is hybrid first, measured always: integrate, benchmark on target hardware, then decide.

t: OpenQuantumSafe: Hybrid Cryptography: Belt and Suspenders
title: OpenQuantumSafe: Hybrid Cryptography: Belt and Suspenders
description: Hybrid key exchange (X25519+ML-KEM) is the migration's safety net: the combined secret is secure if either component holds — against classical attackers via X25519, against quantum attackers via ML-KEM. Standards (and browsers) converged on hybrids for the transition. The combiner is the critical detail: concatenate-then-KDF, done right. Hybrids let you deploy PQC now without betting the farm on new math.

t: OpenQuantumSafe: Constant-Time Code and Side Channels
title: OpenQuantumSafe: Constant-Time Code and Side Channels
description: PQC implementations must be constant-time: lattice operations with secret-dependent branches or memory access leak keys through timing and cache side channels. liboqs's implementations are written (and tested) for constant-time behavior, with the test suite including known-answer and side-channel-oriented checks. The defensive lesson generalizes: the algorithm is half the security; the implementation is the other half.

t: OpenQuantumSafe: Certificates and PKI at PQC Sizes
title: OpenQuantumSafe: Certificates and PKI at PQC Sizes
description: PQC breaks PKI's size assumptions: Dilithium certificates are kilobytes, chains are bigger, and embedded verifiers feel it. The ecosystem adapts: composite certificates (classical+PQC), protocol tuning (TLS record sizing), and careful CA planning. liboqs plus oqs-provider let you build and test PQC PKI today. The CA's migration — root ceremonies with new algorithms — is the program's crown jewel, planned years ahead.

title: OpenQuantumSafe: Debugging: Interop and Negotiation
description: PQC debugging classics: the peer does not offer the group (version/config), the handshake fails on size limits (middleboxes vs big ClientHellos), and the provider does not load (OpenSSL config). The tools are s_client with -groups, packet captures showing the key_share, and the provider's diagnostics. Middlebox intolerance of big handshakes is the real-world friction — test through the actual network path.

title: OpenQuantumSafe: Performance: PQC at Scale
description: PQC performance is a deployment question: ML-KEM operations are fast (faster than ECDH in many implementations), Dilithium signing is fast but verification costs more, and the sizes (keys, signatures, handshakes) dominate the network math. Benchmarks on the target hardware — not the laptop — decide. The good news: for TLS, the handshake cost is usually lost in the noise of the connection.

title: OpenQuantumSafe: Testing: Known-Answer and Wycheproof
description: PQC testing layers: known-answer tests (NIST vectors) for correctness, Wycheproof-style edge cases, interop tests between implementations, and the constant-time checks. liboqs's test suite runs the NIST KATs on every build. For adopters: test your integration against the KATs, test interop against another implementation, and never ship an implementation that fails either.
